title: Why uranium has to be enriched for reactor fuel
examples: How does a centrifuge enrich uranium?
What percentage of reactor fuel is uranium-235?

items.label: Natural uranium
items.ask: Why can't natural uranium be used in most reactors?

explain.say: Uranium dug from the ground is mostly uranium-238. Only about 7 atoms in every thousand are uranium-235, the kind that splits easily, and that is too few to keep a chain reaction going in most reactors.

draw.text: Why uranium has to be enriched for reactor fuel

items.label: Natural uranium
items.ask: Why can't natural uranium be used in most reactors?

explain.say: So the uranium is enriched: the share of uranium-235 is raised to about 3 to 5 percent for ordinary power stations. Then enough neutrons find a uranium-235 nucleus to keep the chain going.

items.label: Natural uranium
items.ask: Why can't natural uranium be used in most reactors?

explain.say: Enrichment spins a gas called uranium hexafluoride in very fast centrifuges. Molecules containing uranium-238 are slightly heavier and drift towards the wall, so gas near the middle is a little richer in uranium-235. The leftover is depleted uranium.

items.label: Natural uranium
items.ask: Why can't natural uranium be used in most reactors?

explain.say: The difference is tiny, under one percent in weight, so the gas passes through long cascades of centrifuges, each enriching it a little more. Some new reactor designs use fuel enriched to just under 20 percent.

items.label: Natural uranium
items.ask: Why can't natural uranium be used in most reactors?

faq.q: Why can't natural uranium be used in most reactors?
faq.a: With only 0.7 percent uranium-235, too many neutrons are absorbed by uranium-238 and ordinary water before they cause another fission. Some reactors, like Canada's CANDU design, manage by using heavy water, which absorbs far fewer neutrons.
Most power reactors use uranium enriched to about 3 to 5 percent uranium-235. It is made into small ceramic pellets stacked inside long metal tubes called fuel rods.
asks: What is in a fuel rod?

faq.q: How does a centrifuge enrich uranium?
faq.a: Uranium hexafluoride gas spins at very high speed inside a tall tube. The slightly heavier uranium-238 molecules drift outwards, so gas taken from nearer the centre has a little more uranium-235. Many centrifuges in a row build up the effect.
Depleted uranium has less uranium-235 than natural uranium, around 0.2 to 0.3 percent. Most is stored, and some is used as a very dense material for counterweights and radiation shielding.

faq.q: Why is uranium turned into a gas?
faq.a: Centrifuges need a gas, so the molecules can move and sort themselves by weight. Uranium hexafluoride turns into a gas at about 56 degrees Celsius, which makes it handy, though it is chemically hazardous.

facts: Natural uranium is about 99.3 percent uranium-238 and 0.7 percent uranium-235.
Uranium hexafluoride turns from a solid straight into a gas at about 56 degrees Celsius at normal pressure.

quiz.why: The two kinds of uranium differ in mass by only about one percent, so each centrifuge changes the mix only slightly.

wrong.1: Each centrifuge holds huge numbers of molecules.
wrong.2: The centrifuges separate by weight; they are not coolers.
